1:
Henry frames the chapter as a reconciliation: God and his servant had parted in anger, the quarrel beginning on Jonah's side when he fled to outrun his work, and the making up begins on God's. He then asks four questions of the verse. When did he pray? In affliction, when the heart is humbled and made serious,; and also when preserved alive by a miracle that plainly indicated he was reserved for further mercy, since an apprehension of God's good-will opens lips that guilt had closed. Where? Anywhere, for no place is amiss for prayer, and though the fish was a close dark dungeon he had freedom of access there, since men may shut us out from communion with one another but not with God. To whom? To the Lord his God, a God in covenant with him, for not every transgression in the covenant throws a man out of it, which is what encourages backsliding children to return. And what? A prayer whose substance he afterwards recollected and left on record, reflecting on the conflict then in his breast between faith and sense, hope and fear.

Gill measures the silence before it. Jonah had been a praying man, but disobedience restrained prayer; all the way to Joppa he did not pray, and Gill asks how he could have the face to pray to the God from whose face he was fleeing. That he prayed in the fish Gill finds marvellous twice over, that he could breathe at all and more that he breathed spiritually. Calvin makes the same contrast his lesson: at liberty Jonah thought he could escape God and became a fugitive, but shut within narrow bounds he prays of his own accord. We may learn, Calvin says, how much it profits us to be drawn back as by cords, since when free we wander beyond all limits; and he presses the harder question, how a man could direct his petitions to the very hand pressing him so heavily. That he could is a wonderful and almost incredible example of faith, and it teaches that heavy affliction is the seasonable time for prayer, though most men will not pray freely unless their minds are calm.

What kind of speech this is divides the voices slightly. Clarke calls the chapter, apart from its first and last verses, a beautiful prayer or hymn made of the thoughts Jonah had in the fish, and answers the objection about breathing in a single stroke: very easily, if God so willed it, since the whole is a miracle from the swallowing to the casting ashore. Ellicott takes it for a psalm of thanksgiving introduced as Hannah's song is. Keil and Delitzsch presses further, that this is not a petition for deliverance but praise for deliverance already received, and denies the inference that it must therefore have been spoken on dry land; finding himself preserved alive inside the fish, Jonah took that for the pledge of his rescue. He reports an older remark that the prophet did not utter these very words in that place and order, but shows what his mind was in its conflict with death, and insists that the phrase his God is not to be passed over, since Jonah prayed to the Lord not merely as the sailors had but as his own God. Gill reads the second verse as spoken to others afterwards. Calvin holds that the prayer was offered in the fish's bowels, and explains the past tenses as a continued act, as though he said, I have called and do call. On the belly of hell Clarke and Ellicott agree that the Hebrew word covers the grave and the under-world rather than hell, Ellicott calling it a forcible figure for imminent death; he adds that the connecting word in the last clause is unnecessary, the sudden change of person being more striking without it.
3:
The mariners threw him, but the prayer says thou didst cast me, and every voice notices the substitution. Gill explains it as deliberate: Jonah knew whom he had offended, who had sent the storm, determined the lot, and overcome the reluctance of the men until they did it; and he neither complains nor censures the act as unrighteous, but mentions it to set off the greatness of his deliverance. Keil and Delitzsch reaches the same point more briefly: the seamen were merely executors of a punishment inflicted by Jehovah. Calvin makes the substitution the whole difficulty of the prayer. It was much to cry to God out of the fish, but far harder to lift the mind in prayer while believing God angry; a man thrown into extreme evils by others may still call upon God, but when all the evil suffered was inflicted by God himself, because the sufferer had tried to shun his call, how is he to penetrate heaven with that obstacle in the way? Jonah's mind, he says, was fixed not on the sailors but on God, which is why the pronouns are emphatic; and he puts the sense as a speech: thou drivest me away in pursuing me, yet to thee I come, for nowhere else is there hope of deliverance.

On the words themselves the readings are small and technical. Ellicott would render didst cast rather than hadst cast, takes the floods for a word literally meaning river and used here of ocean currents, and gives all thy breakers and billows as more exact. Keil and Delitzsch notes that the deep is defined by the heart of the seas as the deepest abyss, and that the plural stands where the singular might, to convey a boundless ocean. Gill infers that Jonah was far from shore in the great deep, which he thinks confirmed by the size of the fish, since so large a creature could swim only in deep water. Clarke alone reads literally a line the others take as figure: while the fish sought food in the paths of the deep, the waves really were rolling above it.

The fourth verse turns from the sea to the fear behind it. Gill guards the sense of being cast out of sight, since Jonah knew the eye of omniscience reached into the fish and the depths; what he thought was that he had passed out from under the eye of providence, and that God would never again look on him with love and pity. These, Gill says, are the words of a man near despair, into which a ray of hope then breaks. Calvin defines the casting away as God allowing a man no access to him, and meets the objection that faith must then have been extinguished. In the struggle of faith, he answers, one thought is suggested and another of opposite character meets it, and there would be no trial of faith without it; when the flesh insists that God is opposed to us and no pardon remains, faith sets up its shield and repels the assault. Ellicott hears reproach in the phrasing, that Jonah had wilfully withdrawn from God's presence and God had taken him at his word; where an older sufferer said only that he was cut off, Jonah uses the stronger word, driven forth and expelled like the mire the waves push along, or as Adam was from Paradise. The last clause he finds impressive in the Hebrew and renders as an exile's hope, that one thing is left him, to turn toward the holy temple and pray. Calvin reports and rejects a negative rendering, that he would look toward the temple no more, since the particle will not bear it, meaning rather truly or nevertheless and sometimes perhaps. Clarke draws a date from the same clause, that Jerusalem was not yet destroyed, since the temple was still standing.
5:
Whether these lines describe a man or a place divides the voices. Clarke reads them literally. The weeds about the head he takes for the seaweed the fish had swallowed as food, among which Jonah found himself; the bottoms of the mountains he explains as the fish following the slanting base of the hills until they ended in a plain at the bottom of the great deep. Gill is nearly as literal, placing the mountains either in mid-sea or in the promontories of the shore, and citing an old writer on the vast rocks overhanging the sea near Joppa, where Jonah was thrown in. Ellicott takes the opposite view. The touch about the weeds he calls quite original, since the figure of overwhelming waters is common in Hebrew song for a crushing sorrow but nowhere else so vivid; and he asks the reader to notice that the fish is never mentioned, as it could not be in a picture of a drowning man tangled in seaweed. The stress, he says, falls not on the mode of escape but on the escape itself.

Gill offers both readings of the compassing waters, either those that nearly suffocated him when first thrown in, or those the fish drew into its belly in quantity enough to endanger his life there. Clarke says only that they seemed to deprive him of life. Calvin fixes the phrase even to the soul as meaning to the peril of life, other explanations being frigid and strained, since the Hebrews say a man is pressed to the soul as the Latins say the bowels are wounded; on the weed he lists sedge, sea-weed and bulrush and judges the sense the same in each. His interest is elsewhere. Jonah kept the wrath of God always before him, knowing the calamity had come for his sins, and the piling up of circumstances shows he could not have lifted his mind to God except by an extraordinary miracle.

On the bars of the earth the voices converge. Calvin places Jonah not in mid-sea but fixed in the deep under the roots of mountains, so that no deliverance could be hoped for unless God stretched out his hand in a manner new and incredible; the bars he explains by scale, since a bolted door is a small thing, and here the whole earth is the door, set against him to keep him from the light of the sun. Ellicott arrives there by another route. Mountains were conceived as the pillars of the world with foundations planted in the sea, so the hidden bases of the hills were the verge of the earth and a man lost among them already close on the under-world; the clause reads literally that the earth's bars were behind him for ever, its gates shut with no return possible. A gateway to the under-world is a common figure, he notes, but the earth is nowhere else said to be guarded so, which has led one scholar to propose an emendation, though he finds it as natural to imagine a guarded passage out of the land of the living as into the land of the dead; and for corruption he would read pit. Clarke pictures a prisoner in a dungeon barred in with bolts he cannot move, which at first seemed to be for ever. On the turn that follows, Clarke suggests the prayer was composed in substance inside the fish and afterwards thrown into verse with some circumstances added, this clause among them, since it speaks of a danger already past. Calvin marks the wording instead: Jonah does not say thou hast delivered me but thou hast brought up my life from the pit, testifying that he was not merely rescued but raised from the dead by a kind of resurrection; and he would not have said my God unless persuaded of his fatherly love.
7:
The fainting soul is described three ways that agree. Gill takes it of a mind covered with grief and overwhelmed with sorrow, ready to sink at the sight of its own sins and under a sense of God's displeasure. Ellicott gives the literal sense, that the soul covered itself, the same Hebrew word being rendered overwhelmed elsewhere, and thinks of the blinding mist of death stealing slowly over sight and sense. Calvin works the same root harder. It means to hide or cover, and though in this form it is usually taken as to fail, he would keep the older sense and read that the soul rolled itself up, as another sufferer is said to roll himself up in his distress; a rendering that makes it multiplied prayers he dismisses as unsupported. What the phrase describes, he says, is what happens when a man is tossed about by various thoughts and left bound up in a hopeless condition: the soul folds in on itself, and all the thoughts of a man in perplexity recoil upon him, so that whatever he strives to push away comes back on his own head. Two things follow for Calvin. Jonah came through only with the greatest difficulty, not until his soul had actually fainted; and even so he sought God, since the remembering here proceeded from faith, whereas the ungodly also remember God but only dread him.

Clarke reads the second clause as a picture rather than a report. Prayer is personified, sent out as a messenger from the distressed man, entering the temple and standing before God, which he calls a very fine and delicate image; and this clause he counts among those the prophet added when he came to write the prayer down.

The proverb about lying vanities is applied narrowly or broadly according to the voice. Gill reports that the old versions and most interpreters take it of idolaters in general, and that one commentator refers it to the mariners of the ship, who promised to give up their idols and to sacrifice to the Lord and did neither; but he thinks Jonah is reflecting chiefly on himself, and leaving a general instruction to any who should likewise give way to an evil heart of unbelief and consult with flesh and blood. Calvin reports the same reading about the sailors and calls it too forced, along with another that turns on a second sense of the word, by which penitents restored to a sound mind relinquish their own reproach; that is true in itself, he grants, but too strained here. His own view is that Jonah sets his religion against the inventions men contrive for themselves, and he notes that the word for vanity means vapour or smoke or breath and in the plural is commonly applied to idols. Clarke widens the charge past idols proper to those who follow vain predictions or let themselves be governed by foolish fears until they leave the path of obvious duty; in leaving the God who is the fountain of mercy, he says, they abandon the measure of mercy he had treasured up for them. Ellicott makes the loss contractual: to forsake their own mercy is to forfeit their share of the covenant grace, for though the Lord does not forsake his own, they by forsaking him and his law can forfeit the privilege. Calvin states it most absolutely, that as soon as men depart from God they depart from life and salvation, and keep nothing, having wilfully cast away every good that could be hoped or desired.
9:
Gill takes the vow for both the legal offering Jonah would bring at Jerusalem and the spiritual sacrifice of praise offered with it, which he knew was the more acceptable. Clarke reads it as a promise to be executed as soon as circumstances allowed, which is why the next clause adds that he will pay what he vowed; and on the closing words he spreads the sense wide, that deliverance from danger and redemption of the soul from the guilt of sin alike are from the Lord, who alone is Saviour. Ellicott renders the line as deliverance is Jehovah's, and places Jonah on the other side of the proverb just quoted: he has sinned, but is still of the covenant people, and by sacrifice can be formally restored to the favour repentance regained. Calvin makes the vow a defence. Our minds being prone to falsehood, any new superstition will take hold unless we are held by this one bond, a settled persuasion that salvation dwells in God alone; once fixed, that conviction is not easily lost though Satan spread his allurements on every side. Jonah, knowing himself as prone to error as any man, was strengthening himself to persevere. He adds that worship consists especially in praise, since God counts all sacrifices as nothing except they set forth the praise of his name; Jonah might as simply have said, Lord, I ascribe to thee my preserved life.

On the last verse everything turns on the word spake. Gill observes that he who made the fish could command it, and that his providence brought it near the shore and so wrought upon it that it could not keep its prisoner; he would render the opening as then the Lord spake, after the prayer was finished. Keil and Delitzsch infers the nature of that speaking from the verb that follows, and quotes an early writer that the creature was again impelled by a divine and secret power; the land, he adds, was the coast near Joppa. Calvin counts the miracles rather than the words. That Jonah was not smothered is beyond nature, since fish continually draw in water and a man can hardly live a minute without breathing; that the fish came to shore required God to draw it there, and more to open its mouth. The word said is chosen deliberately, he says, since a report of God's kindness would have been far less emphatic than a word of command; and because the deliverance is an image of the resurrection, it points to the power by which the world was made, and by which we shall one day be raised.

Clarke uses the same verse against a rationalising reading he sets out and refuses: that Jonah swam into a fishing creek, lay entangled among weeds, barely escaped, and afterwards composed this poem in metaphor. The Hebrew word bears no such meaning, he answers, and the gloss is contrary to the letter of the text and to the purpose of the miracle, since Jonah was given as a sign of a resurrection, and such readings deny the sign and the thing signified together; some men, he adds, because they cannot work a miracle themselves, can hardly believe God can. Henry draws three lessons. It shows God's power over all creatures, his ready obedient servants, whereas to man he speaks once and twice and is not regarded. It shows his mercy to a poor penitent, since Jonah had done very foolishly and was not wholly cured by this correction, and yet at his praying a miracle was wrought in nature, to intimate what a miracle of free grace the reception of returning sinners is. And it is a type of the resurrection of Christ, who lay three days a prisoner for our debt and came forth on the third day, as Jonah did, to send out the preaching of repentance and remission.
